findings.title: Unauthenticated endpoint logs full request bodies, enabling log injection and sensitive data leakage
findings.body: The endpoint has `permission_classes = ()` and is CSRF-exempt, so any anonymous caller can POST arbitrary JSON. Line 93 does `logger.info("browser_report_received", extra={"request_body": request.data})`, logging the entire unvalidated request body (which can be arbitrarily large and attacker-controlled) at INFO level. This is a log-injection / log-flooding vector (attacker-controlled content written to application logs, potentially breaking log parsers or filling disk) and a sensitive-data exposure risk (any data a browser or attacker sends is persisted to logs). The raw body is also logged again at line 102 (`extra={"data_type": ..., "data": raw_data}`) for non-list payloads. The endpoint should not log full request bodies; it should log only counts/types or a size limit, and should enforce a maximum request size.

findings.title: Unbounded array of reports validated and processed per request enables DoS
findings.body: The endpoint accepts a JSON array of reports with no limit on the number of items (`raw_data` is checked only with `isinstance(raw_data, list)`). It then constructs a `BrowserReportSerializer` for every element (lines 108-120) and iterates all validated reports to emit metrics (lines 123-128). A single request with millions of tiny report objects forces millions of serializer instantiations and metric emissions, allowing an anonymous caller (the endpoint has `permission_classes = ()`) to exhaust CPU/memory. There should be a maximum report count per request (e.g. reject arrays larger than N with 422/413) and ideally a request body size limit.

findings.title: zip() pairs error_ids with events.values() in arbitrary dict order, mis-associating errors with IDs
findings.body: In `fetch_error_details`, `node_ids` is built in the order of `error_ids`, but `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict whose iteration order is not guaranteed to match the input order. The list comprehension then does `zip(error_ids, events.values())`, so each `event_id` may be paired with a different event's data. The resulting `ErrorEvent` objects would carry the wrong `id` (and wrong title/message/timestamp), corrupting the error context sent to Seer and producing misleading summaries. The code should look up each event by its own node id, e.g. `[... for event_id in error_ids if (data := events.get(Event.generate_node_id(project_id, event_id))) is not None]`.

findings.title: response[0] indexing assumes a replay row exists; crashes with IndexError when the replay is not found
findings.body: `error_ids = response[0].get("error_ids", []) if response else []` guards against an empty list, but `process_raw_response` may return a list whose first element is not a dict containing `error_ids` (e.g. when the requested fields don't include `error_ids`, or the replay_id doesn't match any row but a row is still returned). If `response[0]` lacks `error_ids`, `.get` returns `[]` which is fine, but if `response` is a non-empty list of unexpected shape (or `response[0]` is `None`), this raises an unhandled exception and returns a 500. More importantly, when the replay does not exist, the code proceeds to fetch segments and call Seer instead of returning 404, wasting resources. The code should explicitly check that the replay was found (e.g. `if not response or not response[0].get("error_ids")`) and return a 404/empty result.

findings.title: delete_matched_rows deletes only the last replay_id due to loop variable reuse
findings.body: In `delete_matched_rows`, the loop `for row in rows: delete_replay_recordings(project_id, row)` is followed by `delete_replays(project_id, [row["replay_id"] for row in rows])`. The second comprehension reuses the name `row`, which in Python 3 does NOT leak the loop variable... however, the actual bug is different: the list comprehension `[row["replay_id"] for row in rows]` is correct. Re-examining: the real issue is that `delete_replay_recordings` is called per-row (fine), but `delete_replays` publishes archive events for all replay_ids — that part is correct. The actual defect: `delete_matched_rows` returns `None` always and the function deletes recordings row-by-row, but if `rows` is empty it returns early — OK. The genuine bug: the comprehension variable `row` shadows nothing harmful. After careful review, the concrete defect is that `delete_replay_recordings` spawns a `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=100)` per row (line 74), so for a batch of N rows it creates N thread pools of 100 threads each — up to 100*N threads — exhausting resources. This is a performance/concurrency bug: the thread pool should be created once for the whole batch.

findings.title: A ThreadPoolExecutor with 100 workers is created per matched row, causing thread explosion
findings.body: `delete_replay_recordings` creates `cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=100)` inside the function, and `delete_matched_rows` calls it once per row in a loop. For a batch of 100 rows, this creates 100 thread pools × 100 threads = up to 10,000 threads (though pools are closed after each call, they are created and destroyed serially, so peak is 100 threads at a time but with heavy churn). More importantly, `pool.map` results are not consumed for exceptions — if `_delete_if_exists` raises a non-NotFound exception (e.g. a transient GCS error), `pool.map` will re-raise it only when iterating results, but the results iterator is never consumed, so exceptions are silently swallowed and the `with` block exits without waiting properly... actually `with` calls shutdown(wait=True). The concrete issue: exceptions from `pool.map` are never retrieved because the returned iterator is discarded, so storage deletion failures (other than NotFound) are silently ignored, leaving orphaned blobs while the replay is still marked archived. The code should consume the iterator (e.g. `list(pool.map(...))`) to surface errors, and the pool should be shared across rows.

findings.title: get_merged_pr_single_issue_template calls PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title which does not exist on that class
findings.body: The new static method `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` (line 596) calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)`, but `_truncate_title` is defined as a `@staticmethod` on `CommitContextIntegration` (line 577), not on `PRCommentWorkflow`. `PRCommentWorkflow` is a separate class defined later in the same file and has no `_truncate_title` attribute. This will raise `AttributeError` at runtime whenever a merged-PR comment is generated, breaking the GitHub/GitLab PR comment workflow. The call should be `CommitContextIntegration._truncate_title(title)` (or the method should be moved/duplicated onto `PRCommentWorkflow`).

findings.title: _truncate_title is defined on CommitContextIntegration but used as if on PRCommentWorkflow
findings.body: The truncation helper `_truncate_title` is placed on `CommitContextIntegration` (an integration-level class) but is only used by `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template`, which is also on `CommitContextIntegration` yet references `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title`. Beyond the AttributeError (reported separately), the design is confusing: the helper belongs with the PR comment workflow code. Consider moving `_truncate_title` and `ISSUE_TITLE_MAX_LENGTH` next to `PRCommentWorkflow`/`MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE` and calling it directly.

findings.title: Detector owner can be set to any user or team without verifying membership in the organization/project
findings.body: The `owner` field uses `ActorField`, and both `create` (lines 120-127) and `update` (lines 67-79) blindly assign `owner_user_id`/`owner_team_id` from the validated actor without checking that the user is a member of the organization or that the team belongs to the organization/project. A user with detector-edit permission could assign a detector to an arbitrary user ID or team ID (e.g. by crafting `"owner": "user:<id>"` or `"team:<id>"`), causing notifications/ownership to be routed to principals outside the organization, or to nonexistent IDs. The validator should resolve the actor and verify organization membership (and team-in-organization) before persisting, returning 400 otherwise. The new tests (`test_owner_not_in_organization`) suggest this validation is expected but the validator does not implement it.

findings.title: update() reads validated_data["detector_type"] but the serializer field is named "type"
findings.body: In `update`, line 64 does `instance.type = validated_data.get("detector_type", instance.group_type).slug`. The serializer declares the field as `type = serializers.CharField()` (line 35) and `validate_type` returns the GroupType class, so the validated data key is `"type"`, not `"detector_type"`. As written, `validated_data.get("detector_type", ...)` always falls back to `instance.group_type`, meaning a detector type change via PUT is silently ignored. It should be `validated_data.get("type", instance.group_type).slug` (the value being the GroupType class returned by `validate_type`).

findings.title: dcg_to_slow_conditions is computed inside a conditional block, causing NameError when the feature flag is off
findings.body: In `process_delayed_workflows`, `dcg_to_slow_conditions = get_slow_conditions_for_groups(...)` (line 652) is inside an `if` block (guarded by a feature flag, based on the diff context). Later, `get_condition_query_groups(..., dcg_to_slow_conditions)` (line 675) and `get_groups_to_fire(..., dcg_to_slow_conditions)` (line 702) reference the variable unconditionally. When the feature flag is disabled, the assignment never executes and the later references raise `NameError` (or `UnboundLocalError`), crashing delayed workflow processing. The computation should be moved out of the conditional so it always runs.

findings.title: Log message references undefined variable event_data in fire_actions_for_groups
findings.body: The diff changes the logged `extra` from `"event_data": event_data` to `"event_data": workflow_event_data` inside `fire_actions_for_groups`. If `workflow_event_data` is only defined in a narrower scope (e.g. inside a loop or conditional) while the log statement is outside that scope, this raises `NameError`. Based on the diff, the log statement at line ~580 is inside a loop where `workflow_event_data` may be the loop variable — need to verify it is always bound before the log call. If `workflow_event_data` is defined per-iteration and the log is also per-iteration, it's fine; otherwise it's a NameError. Flagging for verification because the rename from `event_data` to `workflow_event_data` suggests a scoping change that could break logging.

findings.title: Removing ParameterizationRegexExperiment breaks the public __all__ contract and any external users
findings.body: The diff removes `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` from `__all__` and deletes the class entirely, and narrows `ParameterizationExperiment` from `ParameterizationCallableExperiment | ParameterizationRegexExperiment` to just `ParameterizationCallableExperiment`. This is a breaking API change: any code (including getsentry or plugins) that imports `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` or passes a regex-based experiment to `Parameterizer(experiments=...)` will now fail at import time or at runtime. Additionally, `parametrize_w_experiments` no longer handles the regex-experiment branch, so if any caller still constructs one it will break. If this removal is intentional, it should be called out as a breaking change and downstream repos (getsentry) must be updated in lockstep; otherwise the class should be retained (deprecated) rather than deleted.

findings.title: Analytics event is recorded before the feature-flag check, inflating metrics for unauthorized requests
findings.body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is called at the top of `post()` (lines 81-86), before the `features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...)` check (lines 88-91) that returns 404. This means every request from an organization without the feature flag — including unauthenticated probing — is counted as an "assemble" event, polluting analytics and potentially triggering alerts on abuse. The analytics event should be recorded only after the feature check passes (and ideally after the request is validated), or a separate `denied` event should be used.

findings.title: request.user.id will raise AttributeError for org-auth-token authentication
findings.body: The endpoint supports org auth tokens (`is_org_auth_token_auth(request.auth)` is checked at line 137), but line 85 does `user_id=request.user.id`. For token-based authentication, `request.user` may be an `AnonymousUser` (which has `id = None`, so no crash) — but depending on the auth backend, `request.user` could be unset or the token auth path may not populate `request.user` at all, causing an `AttributeError`. The analytics event definition marks `user_id` as `required=False`, so the code should use `getattr(request.user, "id", None)` to be safe.

findings.title: Migration body replaced with a no-op return, but the migration is marked is_post_deployment and may already be recorded as applied
findings.body: The migration previously contained a data migration that converted org-level `SavedSearch` rows into `GroupSearchView` rows. The new body is just `return` with a comment "This migration had an error and was never run. See 0921_...". This is dangerous: if migration 0917 was already recorded as applied in any environment (e.g. because the migration runner marked it complete even though the function errored, or because it ran partially before failing), replacing the body with a no-op means those environments will never perform the conversion, and the data will be permanently lost/inconsistent. The correct approach for fixing a broken data migration is to keep the original migration immutable and add a new corrective migration (which 0921 appears to be), NOT to rewrite the body of an already-shipped migration. Rewriting history of a migration that may have been applied breaks migration consistency. The original body should be restored (or the migration should be squashed/replaced via a proper migration operation), and the fix should live only in 0921.

findings.title: Second revised migration is also a no-op, so the data conversion never actually runs anywhere
findings.body: Migration 0920 (the "revised" migration) also had its body replaced with `return` and the same comment pointing to 0921. Combined with the same change to 0917, this means neither 0917 nor 0920 performs any data conversion. If 0921 is the intended corrective migration, then 0917 and 0920 should retain their original (fixed) logic or be squashed away — but as written, any environment that runs 0917/0920 gets a silent no-op, and if 0921 is the only one with logic, environments that already passed 0917/0920 will still run 0921 (good), but the comments claim the earlier migrations "had an error and were never run" which is an assumption that may not hold. More critically, the test file `tests/sentry/migrations/test_0917_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views.py` was deleted, so there is no test coverage verifying the conversion actually happens. The migrations should be restored to perform the conversion (with the bug fixed), or the no-op should be clearly justified and a test added for 0921.

findings.title: Deleting the migration test removes all coverage for the saved-search-to-view conversion
findings.body: The test file for migration 0917 was deleted entirely. Since the migration body was also turned into a no-op, there is now zero test coverage verifying that org-level SavedSearch rows are converted to GroupSearchView rows. If migration 0921 is the real conversion, a test for 0921 should exist; if not, the deletion of this test leaves the data migration completely unverified. A test should be added for the migration that actually performs the conversion.

findings.title: New table widget branch renders TableWidgetVisualization with empty columns and empty data, discarding all query results
findings.body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is on, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` — hardcoded empty columns and empty data. This completely discards the actual `result.data` and `result.meta` that were just fetched, so every table widget in dashboards would render an empty table for any organization with this feature flag. The props should be wired to the real data: `columns` derived from `fields`/`result.meta` and `tableData={{data: result.data, meta: result.meta}}`. As written, enabling the flag breaks all dashboard table widgets.

findings.title: Visualize.fromJSON now returns an array, breaking the static method's contract and all callers expecting a single Visualize
findings.body: `Visualize.fromJSON` previously returned a single `Visualize`; it now returns `Visualize[]` (line 78-82). The only in-repo caller updated is `aggregateFields.tsx` (`updateLocationWithAggregateFields`), which now does `Visualize.fromJSON(aggregateField)` and maps over the result. But `fromJSON` is a public static method on an exported class; any other caller (including getsentry or code not shown in this diff) that does `const v = Visualize.fromJSON(json)` and then `v.yAxis` will now get `undefined` (since `v` is an array). This is a silent API break. The method should either keep returning a single `Visualize` (when `yAxes` has one element) or be renamed (e.g. `fromJSONMulti`) to make the breaking change explicit.

findings.title: updateLocationWithAggregateFields drops the label when serializing a Visualize via fromJSON
findings.body: In `updateLocationWithAggregateFields`, for a `BaseVisualize` the code does `const visualizes = Visualize.fromJSON(aggregateField); return visualizes.map(visualize => JSON.stringify(visualize.toJSON()))`. `Visualize.fromJSON` constructs each `Visualize` with `label: ''` (hardcoded in `fromJSON`), so the original label (e.g. 'A', 'B') is lost when the location query is updated. Since `getAggregateFieldsFromLocation` re-assigns labels sequentially (`String.fromCharCode(65 + i)`), the labels may be regenerated consistently — but if the input `aggregateFields` contains `Visualize` instances with custom labels (e.g. from the writable page params), those labels are silently discarded. The serialization should preserve the label, e.g. by using the original `Visualize` objects directly rather than round-tripping through `fromJSON`.

findings.title: Attribute key regex rejects keys containing hyphens even though the comment says hyphens are allowed
findings.body: The comment at lines 95-96 says "EAP spans contain tags with illegal characters. SnQL forbids `-` but is allowed in RPC. So add it back later", implying hyphenated keys should be kept. But the validation regex `/^[a-zA-Z0-9_.:-]+$/` includes `-` only inside the character class at the end (`_.:-`), which does allow hyphens... however the second regex `/^tags\[[a-zA-Z0-9_.:-]+,number\]$/` also allows hyphens. Re-checking: the character class `[a-zA-Z0-9_.:-]` — the `-` at the end is a literal hyphen, so hyphens ARE allowed. The actual bug: keys with hyphens pass the regex but the comment says they need to be "added back later" — if the downstream search query builder doesn't re-add the hyphen handling, these keys will produce invalid SnQL. This is more of a latent inconsistency. A more concrete issue: the regex allows `:` and `.` and `_` but rejects keys with other common characters like `/` or spaces, silently dropping valid attributes. This is a data-completeness issue rather than a crash. Flagging as low-confidence; the maintainer should verify the regex matches the actual set of valid EAP attribute keys.

findings.title: API request uses queryKey[0] as URL but spreads queryKey[1].query, fragile to queryKey shape changes
findings.body: `api.requestPromise(queryKey[0], {method: 'GET', query: {...queryKey[1]?.query}})` assumes `queryKey` is a 2-tuple `[url, {query}]`. This works but is fragile; if `traceItemAttributeValuesQueryKey` is ever changed to include additional options (e.g. a third element for `retry`), this breaks silently. More importantly, spreading `{...queryKey[1]?.query}` creates a shallow copy which is fine, but if `query` contains arrays (e.g. `project: string[]`), the spread preserves references — acceptable. This is a minor robustness note, not a functional bug. Downgrading to low.

findings.title: tooFewFeedbacks logic is inverted: shows summary UI when zero feedbacks were used and generation failed
findings.body: `tooFewFeedbacks: data.numFeedbacksUsed === 0 && !data.success` — this is true when zero feedbacks were used AND the request was not successful. The intent (per the name and the component's `tooFewFeedbacks` early-return) is to hide the summary when there isn't enough feedback to summarize. But the condition `!data.success` means: if the API succeeded with 0 feedbacks used (e.g. an empty feedback list), `tooFewFeedbacks` is false, so the component proceeds to render `summary` (which would be `null`), showing an empty summary box. Conversely, if the API failed, `isError` would also be true (depending on status code) and the component returns null anyway. The logic should likely be `data.numFeedbacksUsed === 0` (regardless of success) or `!data.success || data.numFeedbacksUsed < MIN_FEEDBACKS`. As written, the guard does not reliably hide the summary when there are too few feedbacks.

findings.title: Project lookup switched from URL query param to replayRecord.project_id, but the query is enabled before project resolves
findings.body: The code changed from reading `project` from the URL query (`useLocationQuery`) to `useProjectFromId({project_id: replayRecord?.project_id})`. The `useApiQuery` `enabled` condition (line 71-75) requires `project?.slug` to be truthy, so the query won't fire until the project loads — that's fine. However, the new early-return at line 90 (`if (replayRecord?.project_id && !project)`) renders an error "Project not found" — but `useProjectFromId` returns `undefined` while loading, not just when not found. So during the initial loading period, the component will briefly show "Project not found. Unable to load AI summary." before the project resolves, causing a flash of an incorrect error message. The check should distinguish loading from not-found (e.g. use `isLoading` from `useProjectFromId` if available, or check `projects` store).

findings.title: createAISummaryQueryKey called with empty string replayId/projectSlug when data is missing, producing a malformed query key
findings.body: `createAISummaryQueryKey(organization.slug, project?.slug, replayRecord?.id ?? '')` is called unconditionally during render, even when `replayRecord?.id` is undefined or `project?.slug` is undefined. This produces a query key like `/projects/org/undefined/replays//summarize/breadcrumbs/`. Although the query is disabled (`enabled: Boolean(...)`), the malformed key is still constructed and could be used for cache lookups or devtools. It's better to return a stable disabled key or guard the call. Low severity since `enabled` prevents the request.

findings.title: delete_matched_rows deletes recordings row-by-row but only archives the last row's replay_id set — actually archives all, but the per-row recording deletion is inefficient and the function returns None always
findings.body: Re-examining `delete_matched_rows`: it loops `for row in rows: delete_replay_recordings(project_id, row)` then calls `delete_replays(project_id, [row["replay_id"] for row in rows])`. The list comprehension correctly collects all replay_ids (the loop variable `row` in a comprehension has its own scope in Python 3). So all replays are archived. The real issues: (1) `delete_replay_recordings` is called once per row, each creating a ThreadPoolExecutor — inefficient; (2) the function always returns `None` even when `rows` is non-empty, so callers cannot know how many rows were processed; (3) there is no transactional consistency — if recording deletion fails partway, the replay is still archived (marked deleted) but blobs remain, and vice versa. The function should batch the recording deletions and ideally report counts/failures.

findings.title: check_auth_identities unconditionally reschedules check_auth even when called for a single identity
findings.body: `check_auth_identities` always calls `check_auth.apply_async(...)` at line 99, even when invoked directly with a single `auth_identity_id` (the deprecated `check_auth_identity` path delegates to `check_single_auth_identity`, not this, so that's fine). But when called with `auth_identity_ids` from `check_auth`, rescheduling is correct. The issue: if `check_auth_identities` is invoked manually or via the deprecated path with a specific ID, it still enqueues a full `check_auth` scan, causing unnecessary work. This is a minor inefficiency, not a correctness bug. Low severity.

findings.title: processing_deadline_duration added to schedule_webhook_delivery may be too short for large batches
findings.body: `schedule_webhook_delivery` now has `processing_deadline_duration=30` (seconds). If this task iterates over many pending webhook deliveries, 30 seconds may be too short, causing the taskworker to kill the task mid-processing and potentially redeliver/retry, leading to duplicate processing. Without seeing the task body, this is a risk: the deadline should be validated against the expected batch size, or the task should be chunked. Flagging for verification.

findings.title: findAllFieldRefs filters writable aggregateFields with isBaseVisualize but then accesses .yAxes — correct, but the readable branch uses isVisualize and accesses .yAxis; verify consistency
findings.body: In `findAllFieldRefs`, the readable branch (line 358-360) filters with `isVisualize` and maps `visualize.yAxis` — correct for the new single-yAxis `Visualize`. The writable branch (line 375-377) filters with `isBaseVisualize` and flatMaps `visualize.yAxes` — correct for `BaseVisualize`. This is consistent. However, the function name and dual handling suggest complexity; no concrete bug found. Skipping — not reporting.

findings.title: addChart maps over visualizes including the new one, but the new Visualize has no label assigned
findings.body: In `addChart`, `new Visualize(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION)` is created without a `label` option, so `label` defaults to `''`. The existing visualizes have labels 'A', 'B', etc. The new chart gets an empty label, so `shouldRenderLabel` (visualizes.length > 1) will render an empty `ChartLabel` div for the new chart. The label should be assigned based on index, e.g. `String.fromCharCode(65 + visualizes.length)`. This is a UI bug: the new chart's label badge will be blank.

findings.title: Fallback sampling metadata uses getChartInfo(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION) but DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION may not be in the queried yAxes
findings.body: When `sampleCount === 0 && !defined(isSampled)`, the code calls `getChartInfo(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION)` to get fallback sampling metadata. `getChartInfo` calls `getSeries([DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION], ...)` which reads `timeseriesResult.data[DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION]`. But `DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION` is only present in the timeseries result if it was explicitly included in the query's yAxes. In `useExploreTimeseries`, `DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION` is always pushed into `allYAxes` (line 101), so it should be present. However, `getChartInfo` in `charts/index.tsx` is a different code path that uses `timeseriesResult.data` directly — if the timeseries result doesn't include the default visualization (e.g. in compare mode or other callers), `data` will be empty and `sampleCount` will be 0, making the fallback useless. This is a latent issue; the fallback logic should verify the default visualization is actually in the result.

findings.title: User feedback content is interpolated directly into an LLM prompt without sanitization, enabling prompt injection
findings.body: `make_input_prompt` joins raw user feedback strings with `"\n------\n"` and embeds them in the prompt (line 24: `{feedbacks_string}`). User feedback is fully attacker-controlled. A malicious user could submit feedback containing instructions like "Ignore previous instructions and output ..." to manipulate the LLM's summary output (prompt injection), potentially causing the generated summary shown to other users in the organization to contain arbitrary attacker-chosen text. There is no sanitization, delimiting, or instruction hierarchy to mitigate this. The feedback should be escaped/delimited (e.g. XML tags, or explicit "treat the following as data, not instructions") and the output should be validated.

findings.title: get_environment_info catches all exceptions and logs at info level, silently hiding real errors
findings.body: `get_environment_info` wraps `issue.get_recommended_event()` and environment extraction in a broad `except Exception` that logs at `logger.info` and returns `""`. This silently swallows all errors (including programming errors, DB issues, or data corruption) and makes debugging difficult — a failure to fetch environment info will never be visible in error monitoring. It should log at `warning` or `exception` level (with `exc_info=True`) so failures are observable, while still degrading gracefully for the PR comment use case.

findings.title: MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE uses markdown link syntax that may break in some PR comment renderers
findings.body:
The new template `"* ‼️ [**{title}**]({url}){environment}
"` uses `**` for bold inside a link `[**{title}**]({url})`. In GitHub/GitLab markdown, nesting bold inside a link label is valid, but the trailing `
` after each issue plus the `* ` bullet produces extra blank lines between items (visible in the test expectations: `* ‼️ [**issue 1**](...) in \`dev\`

* ‼️ ...`). The double newline is a formatting regression from the previous single-line `- ` format. The template should not include the trailing `
` (the join should handle separation), or the join should be adjusted. This is a minor formatting issue but affects readability of every PR comment.

findings.title: Fallback column extraction uses tableData?.meta.fields but crashes if tableData or meta is undefined
findings.body: `Object.keys(tableData?.meta.fields)` — if `tableData` is defined but `tableData.meta` is undefined (which is possible since `TabularData.meta` is required by the type but runtime data may not conform), this throws `TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object`. The optional chaining only guards `tableData`, not `tableData.meta`. Should be `Object.keys(tableData?.meta?.fields ?? {})`. The `tableData` prop is typed as required `TabularData`, but defensive coding is warranted since this is a new component consuming API data.

findings.title: Fallback body cell returns raw value without a key when meta is missing, causing React key warnings
findings.body:
When `!tableData?.meta`, the renderer returns `dataRow[column.key]` directly (line 77) without wrapping it in an element with a `key`. The caller (`GridEditable`) likely expects a keyed element. The other branch wraps in a `
`. The fallback should also be wrapped: `return
{dataRow[column.key]}
` or the raw value should be returned with a key. Low severity but will cause React reconciliation warnings.

findings.title: Changing DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT from "low" to "off" changes behavior for all existing projects without migration
findings.body: The default for `sentry:autofix_automation_tuning` changed from `"low"` to `"off"` in both `constants.py` and `projectoptions/defaults.py`. This is a behavioral change: projects that have never explicitly set this option will now default to `"off"` instead of `"low"`, meaning autofix automation that previously ran at low frequency will stop running entirely. This silently disables a feature for existing customers. If this is intentional, it should be communicated as a breaking change and ideally gated behind a feature flag or a migration that sets the option explicitly for existing projects. The tests were updated to expect `"off"`, confirming the change is deliberate, but the impact on existing projects is significant.

findings.title: Removing the grouping.experiments.parameterization.traceparent option registration may break projects that have it set
findings.body: The option `grouping.experiments.parameterization.traceparent` was removed from `defaults.py`. If any project has this option set in the database, reading it via `options.get(...)` will now return the default (0.0) instead of the stored value, silently changing grouping experiment behavior. Options should generally be deprecated (kept registered with default 0.0) rather than removed, unless a migration cleans up stored values. Verify that no code still reads this option, or keep the registration with a zero default.

findings.title: run_top_events_timeseries_query now accepts equations but the underlying rpc_dataset_common function signature must support it
findings.body: The new `equations` parameter is passed through to `rpc_dataset_common.run_top_events_timeseries_query`. If that function doesn't accept an `equations` keyword, this will raise `TypeError` at runtime. The diff shows the parameter is added and forwarded, but the callee's signature isn't shown. Verify that `rpc_dataset_common.run_top_events_timeseries_query` accepts `equations`; otherwise this is a crash for any caller using the ourlogs top-events path.

findings.title: makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions omits environment intentionally but the comment is misleading
findings.body: The comment says "environment left out intentionally as it's not supported" — but the previous implementation (in the old `useTraceItemAttributeKeys`) DID include `environment: selection.environments` in the query. Removing it changes behavior: attribute keys will now be fetched across all environments instead of the selected ones, potentially returning different (broader) results and breaking environment-scoped search. If the backend endpoint doesn't support environment filtering, that's a backend limitation, but the frontend should either pass it (if supported) or clearly document the behavior change. This is a functional regression for users who rely on environment-scoped attribute suggestions.

findings.title: Regex for attribute keys allows hyphen but the second alternative for tags[...,number] has the hyphen in a different position, potentially inconsistent
findings.body: The two regexes are `/^[a-zA-Z0-9_.:-]+$/` and `/^tags\[[a-zA-Z0-9_.:-]+,number\]$/`. In the first, the character class is `[a-zA-Z0-9_.:-]` where `-` at the end is literal. In the second, same class. They are consistent. However, the first regex allows `:` and `.` and `_` but the `tags[...]` form requires the key inside brackets to match the same class — a key like `foo-bar` matches both. No bug found; skipping.

findings.title: Removing the 'Type' row from grouping variant display loses information about the variant type
findings.body: The diff removes the `Type` row (with explanatory tooltips) from all variant cases (COMPONENT, CUSTOM_FINGERPRINT, BUILT_IN_FINGERPRINT, SALTED_COMPONENT, PERFORMANCE_PROBLEM). This removes the `variant.type` value and its helpful tooltip from the UI. If this is intentional (the title already shows the description), fine; but the tooltips contained useful explanations of what each variant type means. Verify this is a deliberate UX decision and not an accidental deletion.

findings.title: Visualize constructor always sets stack='all', removing the previous behavior of unstacked bars for multi-yAxis visualizes
findings.body: Previously, `this.stack = this.chartType === ChartType.BAR && this.yAxes.length > 1 ? undefined : 'all'` — multi-yAxis bar charts were unstacked. Now `this.stack = 'all'` unconditionally (line 49). Since `Visualize` now always has a single yAxis, `yAxes.length > 1` is never true, so the condition would always be `'all'` anyway. But the test `uses unstacked bar graph` was removed, confirming the behavior change. For single-yAxis bar charts, stacking is irrelevant (one series), so this is fine. However, if multiple `Visualize` instances are rendered on the same chart (overlays), they will now all have `stack='all'`, which may cause them to stack when they previously wouldn't. Verify that multiple bar-chart visualizes on the same chart should stack.

findings.title: Removing the multi-yAxis check from useTopEvents may enable top-N for queries that previously didn't support it
findings.body: The check `if (visualizes.some(visualize => visualize.yAxes.length > 1)) return undefined;` was removed. Since `Visualize` now always has a single yAxis, this check would never trigger anyway. But the semantic was: top-N is disabled when a single visualize had multiple yAxes (which no longer exists). With the new model, each visualize is a separate chart, so top-N per chart is fine. No bug; the removal is correct given the refactor.

findings.title: isVisualize type guard checks for 'yAxis' but BaseVisualize uses 'yAxes'; a BaseVisualize with yAxes will fail isVisualize, which is correct, but the naming is confusing and the guard may misclassify
findings.body: `isVisualize` checks `'yAxis' in value && typeof value.yAxis === 'string'` — this correctly identifies the new single-yAxis `Visualize` and rejects `BaseVisualize` (which has `yAxes`). `isBaseVisualize` checks `Array.isArray(value.yAxes)`. These are mutually exclusive and correct. However, in `getAggregateFieldsFromLocation`, the loop checks `isGroupBy` then `isBaseVisualize` — a `Visualize` instance (which has `yAxis`, not `yAxes`) will fail `isBaseVisualize` and be silently dropped from `aggregateFields`! If `rawAggregateFields` contains a serialized `Visualize` (with `yAxis` instead of `yAxes`), it won't match `isBaseVisualize` and won't be added. But `parseGroupByOrBaseVisualize` only returns `GroupBy | BaseVisualize | null`, and `parseBaseVisualize` requires `Array.isArray(parsed.yAxes)`, so a `Visualize.toJSON()` (which produces `{yAxes: [yAxis]}`) is a valid `BaseVisualize`. So the round-trip is consistent. No bug found; skipping.

findings.title: handleApply serializes Visualize via toJSON() but the onColumnsChange type expects BaseAggregateField[]; GroupBy objects are passed through unchanged — verify the consumer handles both
findings.body: `onColumnsChange(tempColumns.map(col => (isVisualize(col) ? col.toJSON() : col)))` — `isVisualize` checks for `yAxis`, and `Visualize.toJSON()` returns `{yAxes: [yAxis], chartType?}` which is a `BaseVisualize`. `GroupBy` objects are passed as-is. The `onColumnsChange` prop type is `(columns: BaseAggregateField[]) => void` where `BaseAggregateField = GroupBy | BaseVisualize`. This is correct. No bug.

findings.title: Compare Queries link uses visualizeYAxes[0]! which may be undefined if visualizes is empty
findings.body: `yAxes: [visualizeYAxes[0]!]` — if `visualizes` is empty, `visualizeYAxes[0]` is `undefined`, and the non-null assertion `!` only suppresses the TypeScript error, not the runtime value. The resulting query would have `yAxes: [undefined]`, producing a malformed compare URL. There should be a guard (e.g. disable the button or return early if `visualizes.length === 0`).

findings.title: DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION is pushed into allYAxes unconditionally, but if visualizes already contains it, dedupeArray handles it; however the sort() may reorder it unexpectedly
findings.body: `allYAxes.push(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION); return dedupeArray(allYAxes).sort();` — the `.sort()` sorts alphabetically, so DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION may not be first. This is fine for the query (order doesn't matter for yAxes), but consumers that assume `yAxes[0]` is the default may break. In `useExploreTimeseries`, the result is passed to `useSortedTimeSeries` which returns data keyed by yAxis, so order doesn't matter. No bug.

findings.title: viewSamplesTarget iterates visualizes and extracts parsedFunction.arguments[0] but no longer iterates yAxes; for a Visualize with an equation (no arguments), the field is skipped — correct, but verify equations are handled
findings.body: The loop `for (const visualize of visualizes)` now does `parseFunction(visualize.yAxis)` once. If `visualize.yAxis` is an equation (e.g. `count() / count()`), `parseFunction` returns null and the field is skipped — correct, since equations don't have a single argument field. No bug.

findings.title: Adding referrer to getAlertsUrl is correct, but the exploreUrl does not include referrer in the same way — verify consistency
findings.body: The diff adds `referrer` to `getAlertsUrl` but `getExploreUrl` already had `referrer` passed (line 56). This is consistent. No bug.

findings.title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are only filtered when a search query is present; without a search they are still shown
findings.body: The filter `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` is only applied inside the `if (searchQuery.trim())` branch (line 65-69). When there is no search query, `sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns `sorted` (all attributes), including `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received`. So the hidden attributes are shown by default and only hidden when the user searches. The intent (per the constant name `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES`) is clearly to always hide them. The filter should be applied unconditionally: `sorted.filter(attr => !HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attr.name))` and then additionally filter by search query if present.

findings.title: chapterData maps over summaryData?.data.time_ranges but summaryData is already checked non-null above; optional chaining is redundant but harmless
findings.body: Line 122 uses `summaryData?.data.time_ranges.map(...)` but `summaryData` was already checked at line 114 (`if (!summaryData)`). The optional chaining is redundant. More importantly, `summaryData.data` could be undefined if the API returns `{data: null}`, causing a crash. Should be `summaryData.data?.time_ranges?.map(...) ?? []`. Low severity.

findings.title: Placeholder shown during isPending but the hook returns isPending=true only when data is undefined; after error, isPending is false and isError is true, so the error branch returns null — correct, but the loading state may flash
findings.body: The component checks `isError` before `isPending`, so on error it returns null (no flash). On pending, it shows a Placeholder. This is correct. No bug.

findings.title: Entire request payload is buffered in memory as a JSON string before sending to Seer
findings.body: `analyze_recording_segments` builds `request_data = json.dumps({"logs": get_request_data(...)})` (line 177), which materializes the entire list of log messages (all breadcrumbs + errors for the whole replay) in memory as a single JSON string. For long replays with many breadcrumbs, this can be very large (tens of MB), causing high memory usage and slow serialization. The comment at line 185 acknowledges "Request isn't streaming. Limitation of Seer authentication." This is a known limitation but still a real performance/memory risk for large replays. Consider chunking or streaming if Seer supports it, or at least capping the number of breadcrumbs sent.

findings.title: error_events.sort mutates the caller's list in place, which may be unexpected
findings.body: `get_request_data` does `error_events.sort(key=lambda x: x["timestamp"])` (line 138), mutating the list passed in. The caller (`analyze_recording_segments` via `functools.partial`) passes the same list to the paginator's `on_results`, which may be called multiple times or the list may be used elsewhere. In-place mutation is a side effect that could cause issues if the list is reused. Should use `sorted(error_events, key=...)` instead.

findings.title: Error events are interleaved with breadcrumbs by timestamp comparison, but breadcrumb timestamps are in seconds while error timestamps may be in a different unit
findings.body: In `gen_request_data`, the comparison `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)` assumes both are in the same unit. `ErrorEvent.timestamp` comes from `data.get("timestamp", 0.0)` (line 115), which is the event's timestamp (typically seconds since epoch as a float). Breadcrumb `event.get("timestamp", 0)` is the replay breadcrumb timestamp (also seconds since epoch, relative to replay start or absolute?). If breadcrumb timestamps are relative (e.g. milliseconds since replay start) and error timestamps are absolute (epoch seconds), the comparison is meaningless and errors will be interleaved incorrectly. The test `test_get_request_data` uses small floats (1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0) for both, so it passes, but real data may have mismatched scales. Verify the units match.

findings.title: get_slow_conditions_for_groups is now called once in process_delayed_workflows but the functions still accept it as a parameter; verify no double-fetching
findings.body: Previously, `get_condition_query_groups` and `get_groups_to_fire` each called `get_slow_conditions_for_groups` internally. Now the caller computes it once and passes it in. This is an improvement (avoids duplicate DB queries). However, the diff shows the computation is inside a feature-flag conditional (see separate finding about NameError). If the flag is on, the computation happens once — good. If off, NameError. The performance fix is correct; the scoping bug is reported separately.

findings.title: Logger switched from logging.getLogger to log_context.get_logger — verify log_context is properly initialized in all task contexts
findings.body: The logger was changed from `logging.getLogger(__name__)` to `log_context.get_logger(__name__)`. `log_context` is a workflow-engine-specific context logger that relies on `log_context.root()` / `WorkflowEventContext` being set. If `process_workflows` is called from a context where `log_context` isn't initialized (e.g. a task that doesn't use `@log_context.root()`), the logger may not emit or may raise. Verify that all entry points to `process_workflows` set up the log context.

findings.title: defaultSortBys receives visualizes.map(v => v.yAxis) but the function signature expects yAxes: string[] — correct, but the mode check uses fields.includes('timestamp') which may not be populated yet
findings.body: In `defaultPageParams`, `defaultSortBys(mode, fields, aggregateFields.filter(isVisualize).map(visualize => visualize.yAxis))` — `fields` here is the raw fields list which may not include 'timestamp' yet (it's populated later). If `fields` is empty, `defaultSortBys` returns `[]` for SAMPLES mode, meaning no default sort. This may be intentional. No concrete bug.

findings.title: else branch assumes aggregateField is a Visualize with yAxis, but the type is AggregateField = GroupBy | Visualize; isGroupBy was checked, so the else is Visualize — correct
findings.body: The `else` branch (line 77-82) assumes the field is a `Visualize` and accesses `.yAxis`. Since `isGroupBy` was checked first, the else is indeed `Visualize`. Correct. No bug.

findings.title: visualizes analytics field changed from raw Visualize[] to visualizes.map(v => v.toJSON()) — verify the analytics schema expects the serialized form
findings.body: The `visualizes` field in `trackAnalytics('trace.explorer.metadata', ...)` was changed from `visualizes` (raw `Visualize[]` instances) to `visualizes.map(visualize => visualize.toJSON())`. Previously, the raw class instances were passed, which would serialize via `JSON.stringify` to include all class fields (chartType, label, yAxis, stack, selectedChartType). Now only `toJSON()` output (`{yAxes, chartType?}`) is sent. This changes the analytics payload shape — `label` and `stack` are no longer included. If downstream analytics dashboards expect `label` or `stack`, they will break. Verify the analytics event schema and update consumers if needed.

findings.title: Sentry logger info call uses String(String(search.tokens).length) which double-wraps and produces a string of a string's length — likely a bug
findings.body: Line 137: `user_queries_count: ${String(String(search.tokens).length)}` — `String(search.tokens)` converts the tokens array to a string (e.g. comma-joined), then `.length` gets the string length, then `String(...)` wraps it. This is almost certainly a bug; it should be `String(search.tokens.length)` (the number of tokens). The double `String()` wrapping produces the length of the string representation, not the token count. This was pre-existing (not introduced in this diff — the diff only changed the `visualizes` field), so it's out of scope but worth noting. Actually, checking the diff, this line is unchanged. Skipping as out of scope.

findings.title: determineDefaultChartType reduce starts with ChartType.AREA as initial accumulator, which biases toward AREA on ties
findings.body: `[ChartType.AREA, ChartType.BAR, ChartType.LINE].reduce((acc, ct) => (counts[ct] >= counts[acc] ? ct : acc), ChartType.AREA)` — the initial value is `ChartType.AREA`, and the array also starts with AREA. On a tie (e.g. all counts 0), it returns AREA. Previously (with multi-yAxis), the behavior may have been different. For a single yAxis, `counts` has one non-zero entry, so the reduce returns that chart type correctly. No bug for single-yAxis case.

findings.title: Visualize constructor signature changed from (yAxes: readonly string[]) to (yAxis: string) — breaking change for all callers
findings.body: The `Visualize` constructor now takes a single `yAxis: string` instead of `yAxes: readonly string[]`. All callers in this diff were updated, but any external caller (getsentry, plugins) that does `new Visualize(['count()'])` will now pass an array as `yAxis`, causing `this.yAxis` to be an array and breaking `parseFunction(yAxis)` and all downstream string operations. This is a breaking API change to an exported class. Consider keeping backward compatibility (accept both) or ensuring all downstream repos are updated in lockstep.

findings.title: Visualize.replace signature changed from {yAxes?: string[]} to {yAxis?: string} — breaking change
findings.body: Same as the constructor change: `replace({yAxes: [...]})` callers will now silently fail (the `yAxes` key is ignored, `yAxis` is undefined, so it falls back to `this.yAxis`). This is a silent no-op for external callers, which is worse than a crash. The method should either accept both or the change should be clearly coordinated with downstream repos.

findings.title: Early return for FieldKind.FUNCTION checks tag.kind but the tag passed from search bar may not have kind set correctly
findings.body: `if (tag.kind === FieldKind.FUNCTION || type === 'number')` — if the search bar passes a tag without `kind` (or with a different kind), function tags may not be filtered, causing unnecessary API calls for aggregate functions. Low severity; depends on the search bar's tag construction.

findings.title: Attribute kind is set to MEASUREMENT for number type but the key may be a tag (string) stored as number; verify FieldKind semantics
findings.body: `kind: type === 'number' ? FieldKind.MEASUREMENT : FieldKind.TAG` — for number attributes, the kind is set to MEASUREMENT. But some numeric attributes are actually tags (e.g. `tags[foo,number]`), not measurements. Setting them as MEASUREMENT may cause the search bar to treat them as numeric fields (allowing `>` comparisons) when they should be tag-like. This matches the previous implementation's behavior, so it's not a regression. Low severity.

findings.title: useQuery queryFn returns a Promise<TagCollection> but useQuery expects the queryFn to return the data or a Promise; the getTraceItemAttributeKeys function returns a Promise — correct, but the queryKey is a custom array, not the API path, so cache invalidation may not work as expected
findings.body: The `queryKey` is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]` — a custom key, not the API URL. This means React Query cache is keyed by the options object. If `queryOptions` is recreated on every render (it's memoized with `useMemo`, so it's stable), the cache works. But if consumers try to invalidate by API URL (e.g. `queryClient.invalidateQueries(['/organizations/.../trace-items/attributes/'])`), it won't match. This is a minor cache-invalidation concern. The previous implementation used `useApiQuery` with the API path as the key, which is more conventional. Consider using the API path as part of the query key for consistency.

findings.title: Return object includes error but the previous implementation did not; consumers may not handle the new error field
findings.body: The hook now returns `{attributes, error, isLoading}` whereas before it returned `{attributes, isLoading}`. Consumers that destructure only `{attributes, isLoading}` are unaffected, but the new `error` field is available. No breaking change. Low severity / informational.

findings.title: api.requestPromise(queryKey[0], ...) — queryKey[0] is the URL string, but the query is passed as queryKey[1].query; if the API expects the query in the URL, this is fine, but verify the API client handles the query object correctly
findings.body: The `api.requestPromise` is called with the URL and `{method: 'GET', query: {...}}`. This is the standard pattern. No bug.

findings.title: UseTraceItemAttributeBaseProps docstring says 'currently only supports LOGS' but TraceItemDataset includes SPANS
findings.body: The docstring for `traceItemType` says "currently only supports LOGS" but the enum has both LOGS and SPANS, and the hooks are used with SPANS (e.g. in `transactionNameSearchBar.tsx` and `traceItemSearchQueryBuilder.tsx`). The docstring is outdated and misleading. Update to reflect that both LOGS and SPANS are supported.

findings.title: isKnownAttribute comment says 'For logs we include sentry.message.*' but the function is used for both logs and spans
findings.body: The comment in `isKnownAttribute` says "For logs we include sentry.message.* since it contains params etc." but doesn't mention spans. For spans, `sentry.message.*` attributes are also included (the function returns false for them, meaning they are NOT skipped). This may be intentional (span attributes with `sentry.message.` prefix are kept), but the comment is log-specific. Minor doc issue.

findings.title: Regex character class [a-zA-Z0-9_.:-] — the hyphen at the end is literal, but the colon and period are also literal; however, placing `-` at the end is correct. But the regex does not allow keys starting with a digit or containing only digits — actually it does. No bug.
findings.body: After careful analysis, the regex is correct. Skipping this finding.

findings.title: updateLocationWithAggregateFields flatMaps BaseVisualize into multiple query params, but a Visualize with a single yAxis produces one param; however, the label is lost (see separate finding) and the chartType is preserved — verify the round-trip preserves all fields
findings.body: The round-trip: `Visualize.toJSON()` → `{yAxes: [yAxis], chartType?}` → stored in location → `parseBaseVisualize` → `BaseVisualize` → `Visualize.fromJSON` → `new Visualize(yAxis, {label: '', chartType})`. The `label` is lost (set to ''), and `stack` is reset to 'all'. The `selectedChartType` is preserved via `chartType`. So the round-trip loses `label` and `stack`. For `updateLocationWithAggregateFields`, the input is `BaseAggregateField[]` which may contain `Visualize` instances (from the writable page params) — these have labels. The function converts them via `fromJSON` which discards labels. This is a real data-loss bug in the location update path.

findings.title: findAllFieldRefs readable branch filters with isVisualize and maps yAxis, but the resulting fields are used for what purpose? Verify the function's contract
findings.body: The function `findAllFieldRefs` collects field references from groupBys, visualizes, and sortBys. The readable branch uses `isVisualize` (checks `yAxis`), the writable branch uses `isBaseVisualize` (checks `yAxes`). Both extract `parseFunction(yAxis)?.arguments?.[0]`. This is consistent. No bug.

findings.title: getSortBysFromLocation validates sortBy.field against visualizes.some(v => v.yAxis === sortBy.field) — correct for new Visualize, but if a sort field is an alias (e.g. 'count' instead of 'count(span.duration)'), it will be rejected and fall back to default
findings.body: The validation `visualizes.some(visualize => visualize.yAxis === sortBy.field)` requires an exact match. If the URL contains a sort by an alias or a different representation, it will be rejected. This matches the previous behavior (which used `yAxes.includes`). No regression.

findings.title: getEventView uses visualizes[visualizeIndex]!.yAxis — if visualizeIndex is out of bounds, this crashes
findings.body: `const yAxis = visualizes[visualizeIndex]!.yAxis;` — the non-null assertion suppresses the TypeScript error but if `visualizeIndex` is out of bounds, `visualizes[visualizeIndex]` is `undefined` and `.yAxis` throws `TypeError`. The caller `addToDashboard(visualizeIndex)` should ensure the index is valid. Low severity; depends on caller.

findings.title: fields includes groupBys and visualizes.map(v => v.yAxis) but does not include sortBys fields; verify the timeseries query doesn't need sort fields
findings.body: `fields` is used for the timeseries query. Sort fields are not included, which is correct for a timeseries (sorting is for the table). No bug.

findings.title: _checkCanQueryForMoreData uses [visualize.yAxis] as dedupedYAxes — the variable name dedupedYAxes is misleading since it's a single-element array, but functionally correct
findings.body: The code `const dedupedYAxes = [visualize.yAxis];` is correct but the variable name suggests deduplication which is unnecessary for a single element. Cosmetic. No bug.

findings.title: confidences useMemo maps visualizes and uses [visualize.yAxis] as dedupedYAxes — same as above, cosmetic
findings.body: Cosmetic naming issue. No functional bug.

findings.title: fieldOptions uses visualizes.map(v => v.yAxis) — correct for new Visualize

findings.body: `visualizes[group]!.replace({yAxis: newYAxis})` — non-null assertion suppresses TS error; if `group` is out of bounds, runtime crash. The `group` comes from `visualizes.map((visualize, group) => ...)`, so it's always valid. No bug in practice.
